name: Heian Japan
title: Social Hierarchy of Heian Japan: From Emperor to Base People
period: 794–1185 (the Heian period, in the age of the Fujiwara regents)

tiers.name: The emperor
tiers.you: You reign from the palace in Heian-kyō as head of the court and the state, but you grew up in your Fujiwara mother’s household, and your grandfather the regent decides much of what is done in your name.
tiers.kid: The emperor lived in the palace at Heian-kyō, today’s Kyoto, and led the court, but his Fujiwara relatives held the real power.
tiers.rise: The throne passed by heredity within the imperial family, but in the age of the regents the head of the Fujiwara decided who would reign. Branches of the imperial line grew into clans of their own: the Taira and Minamoto both descended from the imperial family.
tiers.why: The emperor stood at the head of the ritsuryō state and ruled from Heian-kyō, the capital Emperor Kanmu founded in 794 on the model of the Tang capital Chang’an.

tiers.name: The Fujiwara regents
tiers.term: sesshō (regent for a child emperor), kampaku (regent for an adult emperor)
tiers.you: You head the Northern Fujiwara: your daughters are empresses, your grandson sits on the throne, and the business of state passes through your own household’s offices.
tiers.kid: The Fujiwara regents married their daughters to emperors and then ruled Japan in the name of their young grandsons.
tiers.rise: The regency stayed within the Northern Fujiwara, and its hold rested on Fujiwara daughters married into the imperial family. An emperor born of another mother could slip their hold: Emperor Uda regained much of the government, and Emperor Go-Sanjō, from 1068, curbed the Fujiwara and began the rule of retired emperors.
tiers.why: The real power lay with the Fujiwara, descendants of Nakatomi no Kamatari, and their way to it was marriage: Fujiwara daughters became the consorts of emperors, and the clan’s heads were the fathers-in-law, uncles and…

tiers.name: Court nobles
tiers.term: kuge, kugyō (holders of the highest offices)
tiers.you: You hold the fifth court rank or higher, live in Heian-kyō on the rice of your offices and estates, and must answer every occasion with a well-made poem in a fine hand.
tiers.kid: Court nobles lived in the capital, wore robes chosen by their office and the season, and wrote poems for every occasion.
tiers.rise: Rank came largely with birth: the children of high officials were granted a minimal rank of their own, and promotion was slow and bureaucratic. A noble out of favour could lose everything: when the warrior Taira no Kiyomori ruled after 1159, he removed and exiled 45 court officials.
tiers.why: The codes gave every public post a court rank, from the first rank down to the eighth and an initial rank below it, divided into senior and junior and, below the third rank, into upper and lower.

tiers.name: Buddhist monks and Shinto priests
tiers.you: You are a monk of the Tendai monastery on Mount Hiei: you can read and write, study the Lotus Sutra, revere the emperor and the nation, and live on estates that pay no tax.
tiers.kid: Buddhist monks lived in great mountain monasteries near the capital and were among the few people who could read and write.
tiers.rise: Saichō sought the right to ordain Tendai monks independently. Emperors too could take the robe: in 1087 Emperor Shirakawa abdicated and became a Buddhist monk, the first of the cloistered emperors.
tiers.why: Two new schools of Buddhism rose with the Heian court.

tiers.name: Court clerks and menials
tiers.you: You hold the sixth rank and work in one of the court’s offices, as a clerk, a musician or an apothecary, for a rice income a tenth of a fifth-rank noble’s.
tiers.kid: Below the nobles worked the court’s clerks, musicians and doctors, who earned far less rice.
tiers.rise: In the early days of the codes no one could advance beyond the sixth rank except by rare exception, so the line between the fifth and sixth ranks divided the aristocrats from the menials.
tiers.why: Below the fifth rank stood the jige, the ranks from the sixth down to the eighth and the initial rank, held by the menials of the court.

tiers.name: Provincial warriors and local chiefs
tiers.term: gunji (district heads), oryōshi and tsuibushi (the court's provincial warrior posts)
tiers.you: You are a mounted warrior of a provincial family, armed with a powerful bow, guarding an estate for its owner and hoping for a military title from the court.
tiers.kid: In the provinces, local families trained as warriors on horseback with bows and swords: they became the first samurai.
tiers.rise: Regional military families formed around members of the court aristocracy who had become provincial figures, and gained prestige from court-granted military titles; the Taira and Minamoto were among the most prominent. After 1156 warriors took control of court affairs, and in 1185 the Minamoto founded the shogunate at Kamakura.
tiers.why: When Emperor Kanmu abandoned universal conscription in 792, local power holders again became the source of military strength.

tiers.name: Peasants
tiers.you: You grow rice on a field your family has commended to a temple’s estate, so you owe its owner a share of the harvest instead of the provincial governor’s tax and labour.
tiers.kid: Most people were farmers who grew rice and gave part of every harvest to the estate owner or the government.
tiers.rise: A family could commend its fields to an estate for protection from the tax collector, while a debtor who could not pay his rent could lose his land rights and be bound to the estate as a resident cultivator.
tiers.why: Under the codes all land and people belonged to the state.

tiers.name: Base people
tiers.you: You belong to the base people of the codes and wear the colour set for your caste; if you marry one of the good people, your children will be counted among the good people.
tiers.kid: The old laws made some people “base people”, close to slaves, but by around the year 1000 that line had almost disappeared.
tiers.rise: Marriage was the way out: a child of a base and a good parent was counted among the good people.
tiers.why: The codes divided the population into two castes: the ryōmin, the good people, in four sub-castes, and the senmin, the base people, in five sub-castes, close to slaves.
